claim: Transposable elements (TEs) are widespread genomic parasites.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are widespread genomic parasites, and their evolution has remained a critical question in evolutionary genomics.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of TEs in the scientific literature, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The spread of repressive epigenetic marks (histone H3K9me2) to nearby DNA occurs at >50% of euchromatic TEs in D. melanogaster and D. simulans.
source: Surprisingly, the spread of repressive epigenetic marks (histone H3K9me2) to nearby DNA occurs at >50% of euchromatic TEs, and can extend up to 20 kb.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript showing H3K9me2 enrichment around TEs.

claim: The spread of repressive epigenetic marks from euchromatic TEs can extend up to 20 kb.
source: Surprisingly, the spread of repressive epigenetic marks (histone H3K9me2) to nearby DNA occurs at >50% of euchromatic TEs, and can extend up to 20 kb.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq analysis measuring H3K9me2 enrichment at various distances from TEs.

claim: The spread of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs results in differential epigenetic states of genic alleles.
source: This results in differential epigenetic states of genic alleles and, in turn, selection against TEs.
evidence: This is supported by comparing H3K9me2 enrichment at homologous alleles with and without nearby TEs in the two strains analyzed.

claim: Differential epigenetic states of genic alleles caused by TEs result in selection against TEs.
source: This results in differential epigenetic states of genic alleles and, in turn, selection against TEs.
evidence: This is supported by population frequency analysis showing TEs with stronger epigenetic effects have lower population frequencies.

claim: The lower TE content in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster correlates with stronger epigenetic effects of TEs in D. simulans.
source: Interestingly, the lower TE content in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster correlates with stronger epigenetic effects of TEs and higher levels of host genetic factors known to promote epigenetic silencing.
evidence: This is supported by comparative ChIP-seq analysis between the two species showing stronger H3K9me2 enrichment around TEs in D. simulans.

claim: D. simulans has higher levels of host genetic factors known to promote epigenetic silencing compared to D. melanogaster.
source: Interestingly, the lower TE content in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster correlates with stronger epigenetic effects of TEs and higher levels of host genetic factors known to promote epigenetic silencing.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing higher expression of Su(var) genes in D. simulans.

claim: The epigenetic effects of euchromatic TEs play a critical role in the evolution of TEs both within and between species.
source: Our study demonstrates that the epigenetic effects of euchromatic TEs, and host genetic factors modulating such effects, play a critical role in the evolution of TEs both within and between species.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including population frequency analysis and between-species comparisons.

claim: Host genetic factors modulating epigenetic effects play a critical role in the evolution of TEs both within and between species.
source: Our study demonstrates that the epigenetic effects of euchromatic TEs, and host genetic factors modulating such effects, play a critical role in the evolution of TEs both within and between species.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between Su(var) expression levels and TE epigenetic effects between species.

claim: Transposable elements are genetic elements that can copy and transpose themselves into new genomic locations.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are genetic elements that can copy and transpose themselves into new genomic locations.
evidence: This is the standard definition of TEs based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: TEs generally lower host fitness.
source: Even though there are incidental reports of potentially adaptive TEs (Daborn et al., 2002; Schlenke and Begun, 2004; Aminetzach et al., 2005; González et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2010; Mateo et al., 2014; Hof et al., 2016), they generally lower host fitness (Mackay, 1989; Pasyukova et al., 2004) and are widely recognized as 'genomic parasites'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing deleterious effects of TEs.

claim: TEs are widely recognized as 'genomic parasites'.
source: Even though there are incidental reports of potentially adaptive TEs (Daborn et al., 2002; Schlenke and Begun, 2004; Aminetzach et al., 2005; González et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2010; Mateo et al., 2014; Hof et al., 2016), they generally lower host fitness (Mackay, 1989; Pasyukova et al., 2004) and are widely recognized as 'genomic parasites'.
evidence: This represents the consensus view in the field based on established knowledge.

claim: TEs comprise appreciable and highly variable proportions of euchromatic genomes in all eukaryotes surveyed.
source: Despite the deleterious fitness consequences of TEs, they comprise appreciable and highly variable proportions of euchromatic genomes in all eukaryotes surveyed (Biémont, 2010; Elliott and Gregory, 2015; Chalopin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic surveys.

claim: Small RNAs in Drosophila, mammals, and plants are enriched for TE sequences.
source: Small RNAs in Drosophila, mammals, and plants are enriched for TE sequences and regulate the transposition of TEs in host germlines (Girard et al., 2006; Gunawardane et al., 2007; Brennecke et al., 2007; Aravin et al., 2007; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on small RNA composition.

claim: Small RNAs regulate the transposition of TEs in host germlines.
source: Small RNAs in Drosophila, mammals, and plants are enriched for TE sequences and regulate the transposition of TEs in host germlines (Girard et al., 2006; Gunawardane et al., 2007; Brennecke et al., 2007; Aravin et al., 2007; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Measured transposition rates of TEs are significantly higher than excision rates.
source: However, despite the presence of small-RNA regulation, measured transposition rates of TEs are significantly higher than excision rates (reviewed in [Charlesworth and Langley, 1989]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review summarizing empirical measurements.

claim: Euchromatic TE insertions in multiple outbreeding species have low population frequencies.
source: Furthermore, euchromatic TE insertions in multiple outbreeding species have low population frequencies (Charlesworth and Langley, 1989; Dolgin et al., 2008; Lockton et al., 2008; González et al., 2008; Lockton and Gaut, 2010; Cridland et al., 2013; Kofler et al., 2015), and a reduction in transposition rate alone is unlikely to explain such observations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple population genomic studies.

claim: A reduction in transposition rate alone is unlikely to explain the low population frequencies of euchromatic TE insertions.
source: Furthermore, euchromatic TE insertions in multiple outbreeding species have low population frequencies (Charlesworth and Langley, 1989; Dolgin et al., 2008; Lockton et al., 2008; González et al., 2008; Lockton and Gaut, 2010; Cridland et al., 2013; Kofler et al., 2015), and a reduction in transposition rate alone is unlikely to explain such observations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between transposition/excision rates and observed population frequencies.

claim: TEs can be deleterious through inserting into and disrupting genes and other functional elements.
source: It is well-established that TEs can be deleterious through their genetic effects, such as inserting into and disrupting genes and other functional elements (Cooley et al., 1988; Finnegan, 1992), acting as ectopic regulatory elements (Feschotte, 2008), and mediating ectopic recombination that results in detrimental chromosomal rearrangements (Langley et al., 1988; Montgomery et al., 1991; Petrov et al., 2003; Mieczkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating these effects.

claim: TEs can be deleterious through acting as ectopic regulatory elements.
source: It is well-established that TEs can be deleterious through their genetic effects, such as inserting into and disrupting genes and other functional elements (Cooley et al., 1988; Finnegan, 1992), acting as ectopic regulatory elements (Feschotte, 2008), and mediating ectopic recombination that results in detrimental chromosomal rearrangements (Langley et al., 1988; Montgomery et al., 1991; Petrov et al., 2003; Mieczkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TEs can be deleterious through mediating ectopic recombination that results in detrimental chromosomal rearrangements.
source: It is well-established that TEs can be deleterious through their genetic effects, such as inserting into and disrupting genes and other functional elements (Cooley et al., 1988; Finnegan, 1992), acting as ectopic regulatory elements (Feschotte, 2008), and mediating ectopic recombination that results in detrimental chromosomal rearrangements (Langley et al., 1988; Montgomery et al., 1991; Petrov et al., 2003; Mieczkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TE insertions can influence the epigenetic states of adjacent functional sequences, interfering with gene regulation.
source: On the other hand, TE insertions can also influence the epigenetic states of adjacent functional sequences, interfering with gene regulation ('epigenetic effects'; reviewed in [Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: A genome-wide study in A. thaliana first established the associations between DNA methylation of TEs and lower transcript levels of adjacent genes.
source: A genome-wide study in A. thaliana first established the associations between DNA methylation of TEs and lower transcript levels of adjacent genes (Hollister and Gaut, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the specific study.

claim: TEs are a major cause for DNA methylation-enriched regions in the A. thaliana genome.
source: Later studies identified TEs as a major cause for DNA methylation-enriched regions in the A. thaliana genome (Ahmed et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013; Dubin et al., 2015; Quadrana et al., 2016; Kawakatsu et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016), and several demonstrated that this association results from spreading of DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs (Ahmed et al., 2011; Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The association between TEs and DNA methylation-enriched regions results from spreading of DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs.
source: Later studies identified TEs as a major cause for DNA methylation-enriched regions in the A. thaliana genome (Ahmed et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2013; Dubin et al., 2015; Quadrana et al., 2016; Kawakatsu et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016), and several demonstrated that this association results from spreading of DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs (Ahmed et al., 2011; Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies demonstrating causality.

claim: Associations between TEs and enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks were documented in mouse cell lines.
source: Associations between TEs and enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks were also documented in mouse cell lines (Rebollo et al., 2012) and maize (Eichten et al., 2012; West et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study in mouse.

claim: Associations between TEs and enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks were documented in maize.
source: Associations between TEs and enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks were also documented in mouse cell lines (Rebollo et al., 2012) and maize (Eichten et al., 2012; West et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in maize.

claim: TE-induced enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks at functional elements in euchromatin was first solidly supported by comparing the epigenetic states of reporter genes in constructs with and without adjacent TEs in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, TE-induced enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks at functional elements in euchromatin was first solidly supported by comparing the epigenetic states of reporter genes in constructs with and without adjacent TEs (Sentmanat and Elgin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the specific study.

claim: Epigenetic effects of TEs depend on small-RNA targeting.
source: The same study also found that epigenetic effects of TEs depend on small-RNA targeting, and thus on host-directed transcriptional silencing of TEs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Sentmanat and Elgin 2012 study.

claim: Epigenetic effects of TEs depend on host-directed transcriptional silencing of TEs.
source: The same study also found that epigenetic effects of TEs depend on small-RNA targeting, and thus on host-directed transcriptional silencing of TEs.
evidence: This is an inference from the dependence on small-RNA targeting, which mediates transcriptional silencing.

claim: The extent of PEV is influenced by the amount of heterochromatic DNA in a genome.
source: The extent of PEV is influenced by several genetic factors, including the amount of heterochromatic DNA in a genome (reviewed in [Girton and Johansen, 2008]) and heterochromatic enzymatic and structural proteins whose hypomorphic or null mutations enhance or suppress PEV (known as E(var)s and Su(var)s respectively, [Elgin and Reuter, 2013; Swenson et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The extent of PEV is influenced by heterochromatic enzymatic and structural proteins whose hypomorphic or null mutations enhance or suppress PEV.
source: The extent of PEV is influenced by several genetic factors, including the amount of heterochromatic DNA in a genome (reviewed in [Girton and Johansen, 2008]) and heterochromatic enzymatic and structural proteins whose hypomorphic or null mutations enhance or suppress PEV (known as E(var)s and Su(var)s respectively, [Elgin and Reuter, 2013; Swenson et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The epigenetic effects of TEs on an adjacent reporter gene were observed to be contingent on the expression of two Su(var) genes.
source: Likewise, the epigenetic effects of TEs on an adjacent reporter genes were observed to be contingent on the expression of two Su(var) genes (Sentmanat and Elgin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the specific study.

claim: Histone H3K9me3 is enriched around euchromatic TEs in D. melanogaster.
source: Previously, we used D. melanogaster modEncode epigenomic data (Nègre et al., 2011) and demonstrated that histone H3K9me3, a key repressive epigenetic mark, is enriched around euchromatic TEs (Lee 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: TEs adjacent to genes that are highly enriched with H3K9me3 are more strongly selected against.
source: Importantly, TEs adjacent to genes that are highly enriched with H3K9me3 are more strongly selected against, supporting an important role for TE's epigenetic effects in its own population dynamics (Hollister and Gaut, 2009; Lee and Langley 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Euchromatic insertions from most TE families segregate at low population frequencies in D. melanogaster.
source: In this species, euchromatic insertions from most TE families segregate at low population frequencies (Charlesworth and Langley, 1989; Kofler et al., 2012, 2015; Cridland et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple population genomic studies.

claim: Randomly selected, unrelated D. melanogaster individuals usually share few TE insertions.
source: Accordingly, randomly selected, unrelated individuals usually share few TE insertions.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that most TE insertions segregate at low population frequencies.

claim: TEs only comprise 5.4% of the D. melanogaster euchromatic genome.
source: Importantly, TEs only comprise 5.4% of the D. melanogaster euchromatic genome (Hoskins et al., 2015), and the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions can thus be determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genome annotation study.

claim: Euchromatic sequences flanking TEs are enriched for H3K9me2 in the Oregon-R strain.
source: Using modEncode ChIP-seq data generated from the Oregon-R strain, we observed that sequences flanking euchromatic TEs are also enriched for another key heterochromatic histone modification (H3K9me2) and HP1a, while depleted for 'active' histone modifications H3K4me2 and H3K4me3, which are enriched at transcribing promoters (Kouzarides, 2007; Kharchenko et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Euchromatic sequences flanking TEs are enriched for HP1a in the Oregon-R strain.
source: Using modEncode ChIP-seq data generated from the Oregon-R strain, we observed that sequences flanking euchromatic TEs are also enriched for another key heterochromatic histone modification (H3K9me2) and HP1a, while depleted for 'active' histone modifications H3K4me2 and H3K4me3, which are enriched at transcribing promoters (Kouzarides, 2007; Kharchenko et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Euchromatic sequences flanking TEs are depleted for H3K4me2 in the Oregon-R strain.
source: Using modEncode ChIP-seq data generated from the Oregon-R strain, we observed that sequences flanking euchromatic TEs are also enriched for another key heterochromatic histone modification (H3K9me2) and HP1a, while depleted for 'active' histone modifications H3K4me2 and H3K4me3, which are enriched at transcribing promoters (Kouzarides, 2007; Kharchenko et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Euchromatic sequences flanking TEs are depleted for H3K4me3 in the Oregon-R strain.
source: Using modEncode ChIP-seq data generated from the Oregon-R strain, we observed that sequences flanking euchromatic TEs are also enriched for another key heterochromatic histone modification (H3K9me2) and HP1a, while depleted for 'active' histone modifications H3K4me2 and H3K4me3, which are enriched at transcribing promoters (Kouzarides, 2007; Kharchenko et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Enrichment for repressive epigenetic marks around TEs is strongest at the embryonic stage and weaker at later developmental stages.
source: Interestingly, enrichment for repressive epigenetic marks around TEs is strongest at the embryonic stage and weaker at later developmental stages, consistent with our previous study of only H3K9me3 (Lee 2015).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of modEncode data at different developmental stages and citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment in RAL315 and RAL360 strains.
source: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment (Figure 2), which strongly supports the conclusion that these repressive mark enrichments are due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
evidence: This is supported by comparing H3K9me2 enrichment at homologous sequences with and without TEs, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The enrichment of repressive marks around TEs is due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
source: The presence of TEs correlated with substantially higher H3K9me2 enrichment (Figure 2), which strongly supports the conclusion that these repressive mark enrichments are due to TE insertions, and not pre-existing epigenetic states.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of homologous sequences with and without TEs.

claim: 54.2% of 419 euchromatic TEs analyzed were associated with enrichment for H3K9me2 in at least 1 kb of adjacent sequences.
source: Surprisingly, more than half of the euchromatic TEs (54.2% of 419 TEs analyzed) were associated with enrichment for H3K9me2 in at least 1 kb of adjacent sequences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis of RAL315 and RAL360 strains.

claim: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb).
source: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb), and an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: TEs cause an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%).
source: The TE-induced spreading of H3K9me2 in flanking sequence extended for a mean of 4.50 kb (standard deviation 4.59 kb), and an average of 79.8% increase in H3K9me2 enrichment at the TE insertion site (standard deviation 78.8%, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: TEs associated with H3K9me2 enrichment at flanking sequences are not concentrated around pericentromeric or subtelomeric heterochromatin.
source: Our analysis focused on regions far from these heterochromatic regions, and showed that TEs associated with H3K9me2 enrichment at flanking sequences are not concentrated around pericentromeric or subtelomeric heterochromatin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Local repeat density does not differ between TEs that are or are not associated with H3K9me2 spreading.
source: Also, local repeat density does not differ between TEs that are or are not associated with H3K9me2 spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.55).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of local repeat density.

claim: There are no correlations between the extent or magnitude of TE's epigenetic effects and local repeat density.
source: Similarly, we observed no correlations between the extent or magnitude of TE's epigenetic effects and local repeat density (Spearman rank correlation test, p=0.81 (repeat density vs extent of H3K9me2 spread), 0.65 (repeat density vs % increase in H3K9me2)).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Epigenetic influences of TEs are not restricted to specific genomic locations or contexts, and can be observed across diverse euchromatic regions.
source: These results demonstrate that epigenetic influences of TEs are not restricted to specific genomic locations or contexts, and can be observed across diverse euchromatic regions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of association with proximity to heterochromatin or local repeat density.

claim: There is substantial variation in the epigenetic effects of insertions from different TE families.
source: While our results demonstrate that euchromatic TEs have widespread epigenetic effects in D. melanogaster, we also found that the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions vary significantly. In particular, there is substantial variation in the epigenetic effects of insertions from different TE families (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3 comparing different TE families.

claim: LTR-type TE families show a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to other types of TEs.
source: Indeed, LTR-type TE families show a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to other types of TEs (Mann-Whitney U test p=0.00047, median: 0.547 (LTR) vs 0.352 (others), Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 4.

claim: TE families targeted by more piRNAs show more extensive H3K9me2 spreading and enrichment in flanking sequences.
source: Consistently, we observed that TE families targeted by more piRNAs show more extensive H3K9me2 spreading and enrichment in flanking sequences (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: There is no difference in the amount of piRNAs targeting LTR-type TEs compared to other major types of TEs.
source: It is worth noting that there is no difference in the amount of piRNAs targeting LTR-type TEs compared to other major types of TEs (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.19 (wK) and 0.39 (w1118)), suggesting that the observed correlation between the amount of piRNAs and TE's epigenetic effects was unlikely solely driven by stronger epigenetic effects of LTR-type TE families.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of piRNA amounts.

claim: There are no significant associations between the epigenetic effects of TEs and targeting by endo-siRNAs.
source: On the other hand, we did not find significant associations between the epigenetic effects of TEs and targeting by endo-siRNAs (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: TE families with higher copy numbers have larger proportions of insertions with epigenetic effects.
source: Supporting this prediction, TE families with higher copy numbers in a large sample of African flies (Kofler et al., 2015) have larger proportions of insertions with epigenetic effects (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either RAL315 or RAL360 were found in the Zambian population.
source: Consistent with previous genome-wide observations that most TE insertions have low population frequencies in D. melanogaster (González et al., 2008; Kofler et al., 2012, 2015; Cridland et al., 2013), only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either of the two DGRP strains analyzed were found in the Zambian population, and these TEs displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% (first quartile), 0.56% (median), 1.61% (third quartile), Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by population genomic analysis of Zambian flies.

claim: TEs found in the Zambian population displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% first quartile, 0.56% median, 1.61% third quartile).
source: Consistent with previous genome-wide observations that most TE insertions have low population frequencies in D. melanogaster (González et al., 2008; Kofler et al., 2012, 2015; Cridland et al., 2013), only 31.5% of TE insertions present in either of the two DGRP strains analyzed were found in the Zambian population, and these TEs displayed very low population frequencies (0.54% (first quartile), 0.56% (median), 1.61% (third quartile), Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by population frequency analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 compared to high frequency TEs.
source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Low frequency TEs led to more extensive spreading of H3K9me2 compared to high frequency TEs.
source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Low frequency TEs resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment compared to high frequency TEs.
source: Low frequency TEs were more likely to exhibit spreading of H3K9me2 (Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.039, odds ratio = 1.58, Figure 5A), led to more extensive spreading (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.011, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and resulted in a larger increase in H3K9me2 enrichment (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.014, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There are significant negative correlations between the strength of a TE's epigenetic effects and its population frequency.
source: Consistently, by analyzing the population frequencies of individual TE insertions, we observed significant negative correlations between the strength of a TE's epigenetic effects and its population frequency (Spearman rank ρ = −0.15 (extent of H3K9me2 spread) and −0.14 increase in H3K9me2), p<0.005 for both, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recombination rates do not differ between TEs with or without spreading of H3K9me2.
source: However, we observed that recombination rates do not differ between TEs with or without spreading of H3K9me2 (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.83).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of recombination rates.

claim: Neither the extent of H3K9me2 spread nor the increase in H3K9me2 enrichment in flanking sequences was correlated with the local recombination rate for individual TE insertions.
source: Similarly, neither the extent of H3K9me2 spread nor the increase in H3K9me2 enrichment in flanking sequences was correlated with the local recombination rate for individual TE insertions (Spearman rank correlation test, p=0.62 (recombination rate vs extent of H3K9me2 spread) and 0.55 (recombination rate vs % increase in H3K9me2 enrichment)).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Genes in proximity to TEs are more enriched for H3K9me2 within each of the two strains analyzed.
source: Within each of the two strains analyzed, genes in proximity to TEs are more enriched for H3K9me2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations (Lee 2015).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Genes with adjacent TEs have significantly higher, positive z-scores compared to genes distant from TEs in both strains.
source: As expected, genes with adjacent TEs in either strain have significantly higher, positive z-scores compared to genes distant from TEs in both strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by z-score analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For all categories of genes within 10 kb from TEs, z-scores are significantly higher for genes whose neighboring TEs exhibit H3K9me2 spreading.
source: For all categories of genes within 10 kb from TEs, z-scores are significantly higher for genes whose neighboring TEs exhibit H3K9me2 spreading (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There are significant positive correlations between the z-scores of genes and the extent of epigenetic effects from the nearest TEs.
source: Consistently, there are significant positive correlations between the z-scores of genes and the extent of epigenetic effects from the nearest TEs (vs. the extent of H3K9me2 spread: Spearman rank ρ = 0.31, p<10−15; vs. % increase in H3K9me2 enrichment: Spearman rank ρ = 0.30, p<10−15).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Genes whose nearest TEs did not exhibit epigenetic effects have similar z-scores to genes without TEs within 10 kb.
source: It is worth noting that genes whose nearest TEs did not exhibit epigenetic effects have similar z-scores to genes without TEs within 10 kb (dashed line, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The spread of repressive epigenetic marks from euchromatic TEs leads to substantial epigenetic differences at homologous alleles of adjacent coding genes.
source: These observations demonstrate that the spread of repressive epigenetic marks from euchromatic TEs leads to substantial epigenetic differences at homologous alleles of adjacent coding genes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the z-score analysis comparing homologous alleles.

claim: Among genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects, those whose nearest TEs were absent in the Zambian population have significantly higher z-scores than genes adjacent to high frequency TEs.
source: Among these genes, those whose nearest TEs were absent in the Zambian population ('low frequency' TEs, see above) have significantly higher z-scores than genes adjacent to 'high frequency' TEs (Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.0019, median: 0.95 (genes near low frequency TEs) vs 0.32 (genes near high frequency TEs)).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the z-score of a gene and the population frequency of its nearest TE.
source: Consistently, there is a significant negative correlation between the z-score of a gene and the population frequency of its nearest TE (Spearman rank ρ = −0.18, p<10−3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Within either strain, there are significant negative correlations between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels for genes within 10 kb of TEs.
source: Within either strain, there are indeed significant negative correlations between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels for genes within 10 kb of TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.35 (RAL315) and −0.33 (RAL360), p<10−16 for both).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: There is an excess number of genes that support the influence of TE's epigenetic effects on gene expression for genes with TEs within 10 kb when compared to other genes in the genome.
source: We found an excess number of genes that support the influence of TE's epigenetic effects on gene expression (higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression of alleles with adjacent TEs, shaded green area in Figure 7A) for genes with TEs within 10 kb when compared to other genes in the genome (Figure 7B, upper 2 × 2 Tables).
evidence: This is supported by contingency table analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Restricting the analysis to TEs with epigenetic effects produced an even larger proportion of genes whose TE-neighboring alleles have higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression.
source: Restricting the analysis to TEs with epigenetic effects produced an even larger proportion of genes whose TE-neighboring alleles have higher H3K9me2 enrichment and lower expression (Figure 7B, bottom 2 × 2 Tables).
evidence: This is supported by contingency table analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The excess number of genes supporting TE-induced epigenetic effects on expression was mainly observed for one of the two strains analyzed (RAL360).
source: Intriguingly, the excess number of genes supporting TE-induced epigenetic effects on expression was mainly observed for one of the two strains analyzed (RAL360).
evidence: This is observed from the contingency table analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: There is a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs.
source: Furthermore, while we found a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.035, p=0.0084), there are no such correlations observed for genes with TEs within 10 kb (Spearman rank test p=0. 57 (RAL315) and 0.16 (RAL360)).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: There are no correlations between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes with TEs within 10 kb.
source: Furthermore, while we found a weak, but significant, negative correlation between z-scores for H3K9me2 enrichment and fold changes in expression for genes without TEs (Spearman rank ρ = −0.035, p=0.0084), there are no such correlations observed for genes with TEs within 10 kb (Spearman rank test p=0. 57 (RAL315) and 0.16 (RAL360)).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster four million years ago.
source: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster only four million years ago (Obbard et al., 2012), yet is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster (Dowsett and Young, 1982; Vieira et al., 1999; Vieira and Biémont, 2004; Kofler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: D. simulans is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster.
source: D. simulans diverged from D. melanogaster only four million years ago (Obbard et al., 2012), yet is widely observed to harbor fewer TE insertions compared to D. melanogaster (Dowsett and Young, 1982; Vieira et al., 1999; Vieira and Biémont, 2004; Kofler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple comparative studies.

claim: Strong H3K9me2 enrichment is observed in sequences flanking TEs in D. simulans.
source: Similar to D. melanogaster, we observed strong H3K9me2 enrichment in sequences flanking TEs (Figure 8A), and genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis in D. simulans shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In D. simulans, genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs.
source: Similar to D. melanogaster, we observed strong H3K9me2 enrichment in sequences flanking TEs (Figure 8A), and genes adjacent to TEs have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes distant from TEs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In D. simulans, genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes adjacent to TEs without epigenetic effects.
source: Furthermore, genes adjacent to TEs with epigenetic effects (see below) have higher H3K9me2 enrichment than genes adjacent to TEs without epigenetic effects (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: For genes within 10 kb of TEs in D. simulans, there is a strong negative correlation between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels.
source: For genes within 10 kb of TEs, there is also a strong negative correlation between H3K9me2 enrichment and transcript levels (Spearman rank ρ = −0.45, p<10−16), supporting a functional consequence of H3K9me2 enrichment in D. simulans.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data in D. simulans.

claim: There are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread.
source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects compared to D. melanogaster.
source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TE families in D. simulans display a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment compared to D. melanogaster.
source: While there are no significant between-species differences in the extent of H3K9me2 spread (paired MWU test, p=0.67), TE families in D. simulans display a larger proportion of TEs with epigenetic effects (paired MWU test, p=0.013), and a larger increase in relative H3K9me2 fold enrichment (paired MWU test, p=0.035; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TEs in D. simulans exhibit stronger epigenetic effects on flanking sequences compared to D. melanogaster.
source: These results demonstrate that TEs in D. simulans exhibit stronger epigenetic effects on flanking sequences compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative analysis between the two species.

claim: D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats compared to D. melanogaster.
source: Consistent with previous quantitation of simple repeat content using orthogonal approaches (melting curves [Lohe and Brutlag, 1987] or flow cytometry [Bosco et al., 2007]), we observed lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster (Figure 9A, ANOVA p-value=0.00013 (species) and <10−6 (library preparation method)).
evidence: This is supported by K-mer analysis shown in Figure 9A and citations to previous studies.

claim: 40 known Su(var) genes as a group have higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster.
source: Compared to other genes in the genome, 40 known Su(var)s, as a group, have higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<10−6, Figure 9B; also see Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Figure 9—source data 1 for individual genes included in the analysis).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Su(var)3–9 showed significantly higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster.
source: Among these dosage-dependent Su(var)s/E(var)s, Su(var)3–9 showed significantly higher expression in D. simulans than in D. melanogaster (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats and higher expression of Su(var)s compared to D. melanogaster, both of which could account for the stronger epigenetic effects of TEs observed in D. simulans.
source: Overall, we found that D. simulans has lower amounts of H3K9me2-enriched simple repeats and higher expression of Su(var)s compared to D. melanogaster, both of which could account for the stronger epigenetic effects of TEs observed in D. simulans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of heterochromatic DNA content and Su(var) expression.

claim: More than half of euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks.
source: Surprisingly, quantification of the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions in D. melanogaster revealed that more than half of the euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks, with an average spread of 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The average spread of repressive epigenetic marks is 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
source: Surprisingly, quantification of the epigenetic effects of individual TE insertions in D. melanogaster revealed that more than half of the euchromatic TEs analyzed are associated with at least 1 kb spread of repressive epigenetic marks, with an average spread of 4.5 kb from TEs that display epigenetic effects.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Repressive DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs in A. thaliana predominantly spreads only a few hundred base pairs.
source: In contrast, repressive DNA methylation from epigenetically silenced TEs in A. thaliana predominantly spreads only a few hundred base pairs (Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in A. thaliana.

claim: ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain.
source: Since ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain (Kaminker et al., 2002; Quesneville et al., 2005; Hoskins et al., 2015), these estimates suggest that the epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome annotation studies.

claim: The epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
source: Since ~20% of the euchromatic genes are within 5 kb from at least one TE insertion in the reference D. melanogaster strain (Kaminker et al., 2002; Quesneville et al., 2005; Hoskins et al., 2015), these estimates suggest that the epigenetic influence of TEs on functional sequences is extensive in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of genes near TEs and the extent of epigenetic spreading.

claim: TEs contribute significantly to genic DMRs (differential methylated regions) between genomes in Arabidopsis.
source: This concurs with observations in Arabidopsis that TEs contribute significantly to genic DMRs (differential methylated regions) between genomes (Schmitz et al., 2013; Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Arabidopsis.

claim: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila.
source: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila (Cridland et al., 2015; Lee 2015), and the spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for such observations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes.
source: TE-induced reduction in expression of neighboring genes has been demonstrated in Drosophila (Cridland et al., 2015; Lee 2015), and the spreading of repressive epigenetic marks from TEs is a plausible mechanism for such observations.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the observed epigenetic effects.

claim: Recent studies that jointly analyzed mobilomes and transcriptomes in A. thaliana populations found that TE insertions result in equal frequencies of increased and decreased expression of flanking genes.
source: In fact, recent studies that jointly analyzed mobilomes and transcriptomes in A. thaliana populations found that TE insertions result in equal frequencies of increased and decreased expression of flanking genes (Quadrana et al., 2016; Stuart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in A. thaliana.

claim: SNPs and copy number variants (CNVs) in regulatory sequences are identified as significant contributors to differential expression between homologous alleles.
source: Besides, SNPs and copy number variants (CNVs) in regulatory sequences are also identified as significant contributors to differential expression between homologous alleles (Massouras et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks and heterochromatin proteins is high for active genes normally located in the pericentromeric heterochromatin, and is required for the proper expression of these genes.
source: In fact, enrichment of repressive epigenetic marks and heterochromatin proteins is surprisingly high for active genes normally located in the pericentromeric heterochromatin, and is required for the proper expression of these genes (Wakimoto and Hearn, 1990; Hearn et al., 1991; Yasuhara and Wakimoto, 2008; Riddle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a deficiency in the number of genes that both have adjacent TEs and are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos.
source: In fact, we observed a deficiency in the number of genes that both have adjacent TEs and are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos (using data from modEncode (Graveley et al., 2011); Fisher's Exact Test, p=0.00017, odds ratio = 0.73).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The deficiency in genes with adjacent TEs that are expressed in 4–8 hr embryos is even stronger when only considering TEs with epigenetic effects.
source: This deficiency is even stronger when only considering TEs with epigenetic effects (Fisher's Exact Test, p<10−5, odds ratio = 0.58).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Epigenetic marks established at embryonic stages are expected to influence both somatic and germline cells.
source: Epigenetic marks established at embryonic stages are expected to influence both somatic and germline cells, and were experimentally demonstrated to have a long lasting functional effect through development (Gu and Elgin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The observed deficiency in expressed genes with adjacent TEs is consistent with selection preferentially removing TEs that result in spreading of repressive epigenetic marks to adjacent genes expressed in embryonic stages.
source: Accordingly, our observations are consistent with selection preferentially removing TEs that result in spreading of repressive epigenetic marks to adjacent genes expressed in embryonic stages.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed deficiency and the functional consequences of epigenetic marks.

claim: Stable equilibrium of TE copy number in an outbreeding, meiotically recombining population requires synergistic epistasis of the deleterious effects of TEs.
source: In addition, theoretical work suggests that stable equilibrium of TE copy number in an outbreeding, meiotically recombining population requires synergistic epistasis of the deleterious effects of TEs; specifically host fitness must decrease faster than linear with respect to increases in TE copy number (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Synergistic epistasis has only been empirically supported for deleterious effects mediated by ectopic recombination between nonhomologous TE insertions.
source: However, despite being critical to explaining the population dynamics of TEs, synergistic epistasis has only been empirically supported for deleterious effects mediated by ectopic recombination between nonhomologous TE insertions (Langley et al., 1988; Petrov et al., 2003, 2011), one of the many proposed deleterious genetic mechanisms for TEs (reviewed in [Lee and Langley 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The association between the abundance of a TE family and the propensity of its members to influence the epigenetic states of adjacent sequences supports the prediction that deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs confer synergistic epistasis.
source: The observed association between the abundance of a TE family and the propensity of its members to influence the epigenetic states of adjacent sequences supports this prediction, and further extends possible evolutionary mechanisms for stable containment of TE copy number in host populations.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed correlation between TE abundance and epigenetic effects.

claim: The stronger epigenetic effects of TEs in D. simulans could lead to stronger selection removing TE insertions in D. simulans.
source: All else being equal, the stronger epigenetic effects should lead to stronger selection removing TE insertions in D. simulans.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed stronger epigenetic effects in D. simulans.

claim: If the rate of TE proliferation is similar in D. melanogaster and D. simulans, stronger selection in D. simulans could account for the lower genomic TE content in D. simulans.
source: If the rate of TE proliferation is also similar in these two species, this could account for the lower genomic TE content (Clark et al., 2007) and fewer TE insertions (Dowsett and Young, 1982; Vieira et al., 1999; Vieira and Biémont, 2004; Kofler et al., 2015) in D. simulans compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in epigenetic effects and TE content.

claim: Variation in the epigenetic effects of TEs contributes to the divergent TE content observed between even closely related species and significantly impacts TE evolution.
source: Overall, these results strongly support the conclusion that variation in the epigenetic effects of TEs contributes to the divergent TE content observed between even closely related species and significantly impacts TE evolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the between-species comparative analysis.

claim: Su(var)3–9 is a haploid suppressor and triploid enhancer of PEV.
source: Furthermore, Su(var) 3–9 is a haploid suppressor and triploid enhancer of PEV (Schotta et al., 2002), suggesting that changes in transcript levels of Su(var)3–9 would result in quantitative differences in the epigenetic effects of TEs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in transcript levels of Su(var)3–9 would result in quantitative differences in the epigenetic effects of TEs.
source: Furthermore, Su(var) 3–9 is a haploid suppressor and triploid enhancer of PEV (Schotta et al., 2002), suggesting that changes in transcript levels of Su(var)3–9 would result in quantitative differences in the epigenetic effects of TEs.
evidence: This is an inference from the dosage-dependent effects of Su(var)3–9 on PEV.

claim: Variation in the amount of heterochromatic DNA and the expression of Su(var) genes provides a viable explanation for the observed differences in the epigenetic effects of TEs between D. melanogaster and D. simulans.
source: Assuming that the epigenetic effects of TEs depend on the amount of heterochromatic DNA and the expression of Su(var) genes in D. melanogaster and D. simulans similarly, variation in these two genetic PEV modifiers provides a viable explanation for the observed differences in the epigenetic effects of TEs and more broadly divergent TE profiles between these two species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variation in PEV modifiers and their known effects.

claim: The host genetic environment contributes to the extent of deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs and influences the population dynamics of TEs.
source: Our observations support the hypothesis that the host genetic environment contributes to the extent of deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs and influences the population dynamics of TEs, pointing towards a rarely addressed mechanism for the widely observed variation of TEs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed variation in Su(var) expression and heterochromatic DNA content.

claim: PEV is long known to be temperature sensitive.
source: Furthermore, PEV is long known to be temperature sensitive (Gowen and Gay, 1933), and several abiotic factors influence heterochromatin function (Seong et al., 2012; Silver-Morse and Li, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several abiotic factors influence heterochromatin function.
source: Furthermore, PEV is long known to be temperature sensitive (Gowen and Gay, 1933), and several abiotic factors influence heterochromatin function (Seong et al., 2012; Silver-Morse and Li, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different environmental conditions present in diverse habitats could contribute to variation in the epigenetic effects of TEs and the widely divergent TE profiles within and between species.
source: Thus, different environmental conditions present in diverse habitats could also contribute to variation in the epigenetic effects of TEs and the widely divergent TE profiles within and between species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the environmental sensitivity of heterochromatin function.

claim: The deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs are considered as a side effect of host-directed epigenetic silencing of TEs.
source: It is worth noting that the deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs are considered as a side effect of host-directed epigenetic silencing of TEs (Hollister and Gaut, 2009; Lee 2015), and direct positive selection for stronger epigenetic effects of TEs would be unlikely to explain the between-species differences in genetic PEV modifiers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct positive selection for stronger epigenetic effects of TEs would be unlikely to explain the between-species differences in genetic PEV modifiers.
source: It is worth noting that the deleterious epigenetic effects of TEs are considered as a side effect of host-directed epigenetic silencing of TEs (Hollister and Gaut, 2009; Lee 2015), and direct positive selection for stronger epigenetic effects of TEs would be unlikely to explain the between-species differences in genetic PEV modifiers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of epigenetic effects as side effects.

claim: Su(var) genes are highly pleiotropic.
source: Alternatively, Su(var) genes are highly pleiotropic (reviewed in [Girton and Johansen, 2008; Eissenberg and Reuter, 2009; Elgin and Reuter, 2013]), and selection might have acted instead on their essential chromosomal functions, with varying influence on the epigenetic consequences of TEs as a secondary effect.
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Selection might have acted on the essential chromosomal functions of Su(var) genes, with varying influence on the epigenetic consequences of TEs as a secondary effect.
source: Alternatively, Su(var) genes are highly pleiotropic (reviewed in [Girton and Johansen, 2008; Eissenberg and Reuter, 2009; Elgin and Reuter, 2013]), and selection might have acted instead on their essential chromosomal functions, with varying influence on the epigenetic consequences of TEs as a secondary effect.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed variation in Su(var) expression.

claim: The evolution of TEs may be more tightly associated with the evolution of other cellular, chromosomal, and/or genetic processes than previously appreciated.
source: Our findings suggest that the evolution of TEs may be more tightly associated with the evolution of other cellular, chromosomal, and/or genetic processes than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is a broad inference from the observed connections between TE evolution and host genetic factors.
